title: South Carolina Fine Print: BabyNet
description: South Carolina's Early Intervention program, BabyNet, in the state's own words: refer your child yourself, free services, who qualifies, and disputes.
summary: BabyNet in South Carolina's own words: refer yourself, free, who qualifies, and what to do if something goes wrong.
short_answer: In South Carolina, a parent can refer their own child to BabyNet without a doctor's referral, and SCDHHS says the program provides services for free for any eligible child. Eligibility rests on an assessment of the child's skills, BabyNet is part of the state Medicaid agency's Healthy Connections program, and a state complaint must be filed within one year of the alleged violation (a due process hearing request has a longer federal deadline of two years).
h1: South Carolina Fine Print: BabyNet (Early Intervention)
intro: This page is about South Carolina only. I lived this here, and the state describes BabyNet on its own pages. Here is what SCDHHS says, word for word, so you can point to it.

sections.h2: You Can Refer Your Child Yourself, and It Is Free
sections.html:
South Carolina's Early Intervention program is called BabyNet. Many parents wait for a doctor to bring it up. You don't have to.

SCDHHS says: “If a provider does not refer you, you can reach out yourself. A doctor’s referral is not needed.” (scdhhs.gov/babynet)

The BabyNet page has an online referral form and a phone number for the Central Referral team. On cost, South Carolina is clear.

SCDHHS says: “This publicly funded program provides services for free for any child who is eligible.” (scdhhs.gov/babynet)

That matches what I found. The federal rules let some states charge families for certain services, but the Early Intervention fine print explains the difference. In South Carolina, the state's own page says free.

Say: “I would like to refer my child to BabyNet. I do not have a doctor's referral. What do you need from me to start?”

BabyNet decides eligibility by assessing the child, not by waiting for a diagnosis.

SCDHHS says: “Eligibility is based on an assessment of a child’s skills.” (scdhhs.gov/babynet)

SCDHHS says: “If your child has a significant developmental delay or mild/moderate delays in two areas of development, they may qualify for BabyNet. If a child has a physical or mental condition that is likely to result in a developmental delay, they may be eligible too.” (scdhhs.gov/babynet)

If you're not sure whether your child's delay is big enough, make the referral anyway. Let the assessment answer it. The federal evaluation fine print covers what the law says about suspecting a disability.

The first step is an intake appointment. It takes longer than you'd think.

SCDHHS says: “An intake appointment may take up to 1.5 hours.” (scdhhs.gov/babynet)

Bring what you have. The referral asks for documents that are straightforward to gather.

SCDHHS says: “Reason for referral and any known concerns All available related documents Evaluations Medical records Developmental tracking Screenings” (scdhhs.gov/babynet)

My Birth to Three page covers the plan that comes next.

sections.h2: It Is Run by SCDHHS, Not Who You Might Expect
sections.html:
Parents often look for BabyNet in the wrong place. It's part of the state Medicaid agency's Healthy Connections program.

SCDHHS says: “Effective July 1, 2017, BabyNet is part of the South Carolina Department of Health and Human Services' Healthy Connections program.” (scdhhs.gov, BabyNet for families)

The page also notes that BabyNet is South Carolina's Part C program. The Early Intervention fine print explains that federal law.

sections.h2: When Something Goes Wrong: Informal Steps, Then Three Formal Options
sections.html:
South Carolina lays out the steps for a concern. The first two are conversations: talk to the service coordinator or their supervisor, then ask for a meeting of the IFSP team. If that doesn't work, or if you think your family's rights were violated, there are three formal options.

A written state complaint asks the state to investigate.

SCDHHS says: “Written formal state complaints are filed when an investigation is requested to determine if IDEA has been followed.” (scdhhs.gov, disputes and concerns)

SCDHHS says a complaint must be filed within one year of the alleged violation. The federal rule agrees that the one year limit belongs to state complaints.

SCDHHS says: “The complaint must be filed within one year of the alleged violation of rights or regulations.” (scdhhs.gov, disputes and concerns)

The federal rule says: “The complaint must allege a violation that occurred not more than one year prior to the date that the complaint is received” (34 CFR 303.434)

Mediation is voluntary.

SCDHHS says: “Mediation is a voluntary process under Part C of IDEA that brings the parent and others together to resolve disagreements.” (scdhhs.gov, disputes and concerns)

A due process hearing is available to parents and has its own, longer deadline.

SCDHHS says: “A due process hearing can be requested when the parent wants an officer of the court to make a legally binding decision about whether IDEA has been followed.” (scdhhs.gov, disputes and concerns)

The federal rule says: “must request an impartial hearing on their due process complaint within two years of the date the parent, lead agency, or EIS provider knew or should have known about the alleged action that forms the basis of the due process complaint” (34 CFR 303.443)

Federal law also lets a state set its own timeline, so check with BabyNet. Don't wait on any of these. The state asks people to use its Request for Dispute Resolution form, linked from that page. The disagree-in-writing guide has the general approach, and the letters page has a template for the 45 day timeline.

sections.h2: A Way to Ask That Works
sections.html: Start with the friendly step: call the service coordinator, say what you need, and follow up by email so there's a record. Most coordinators carry a heavy caseload, so a clear request is easy to act on. Family Connection of South Carolina offers free help if you want someone to review what you're planning. Check the SCDHHS pages linked below, because phone numbers and forms change.

checked: Every quoted sentence on this page was checked, word for word, against the SCDHHS pages it names (and 34 CFR 303.434 and 303.443 at ecfr.gov for the two deadlines) (scdhhs.gov/babynet, the BabyNet for families page and the Part C disputes and concerns page) on October 5, 2026. Phone numbers, forms and program details change; confirm with BabyNet.
